title: The Steps That Carry a Song
summary: A singer and a relay tradition preserve testimony across an immense burial landscape after officials try to erase valley households.
source_notes: A singer’s development through family composition and changing musical practice becomes the preservation and adaptation of garden testimony.
Endurance sport and assistance between competitors become a relay whose participants confront the difference between winning and carrying someone home.
The destruction of targeted communities and later struggle for acknowledgment inform a fictional valley campaign without borrowing real identities or treating victims as scenery.
A vast burial complex used over many centuries becomes a layered landscape with continuing ordinary labor and competing commemorative claims.

entries.title: Lethra of the Late Measure
entries.body:
Lethra altered her father’s harvest songs to carry missing names. He feared the changes would endanger their household. Their surviving arguments reveal affection and disagreement, preventing later monuments from portraying the repertoire as an uncomplicated inheritance.

Later accounts make Lethra of the Late Measure the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Steps That Carry a Song. Suth’s burial terraces expanded for centuries, accommodating rulers, gardeners, pilgrims, and people denied formal household graves. In 982 a valley campaign classified several gardening communities as supporters of an armed revolt and destroyed their water records. Survivors carried names through sung measures adapted from an older harvesting repertoire. Runners relayed the verses across terraces, sometimes abandoning a timed contest to support an exhausted companion. Later courts trusted official burial inscriptions more than the songs. Comparing the two revealed that prestigious monuments had reused stone from destroyed communal channels. The present dispute concerns testimony embedded in performance and material, neither of which supplies an easy complete account.

In the connected record, [The Hundred Stair Necropolis](b005-the-hundred-stair-necropolis.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Testimony in Measure Rule](b005-the-testimony-in-measure-rule.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: who must maintain the terraces while descendants seek acknowledgment of the gardens their monuments displaced.

Asylum customs let strangers work under temporary names, but temporary recognition does not automatically convey inheritance. The same gardens can preserve an old promise and expose its injustice. entries.title: The Hundred Stair Necropolis
entries.body:
The necropolis includes royal platforms and crowded communal slopes. Gardeners maintain its retaining walls because collapse would bury their fields. Courts call this reverence, ignoring that much of the labor is compelled by geography rather than consent to the monuments above.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Relay of Name Bearers
entries.body:
Relay members memorize overlapping sections, so one lost singer does not erase an entire sequence. Prestige attaches to accuracy and assistance, not speed alone. Wealthy sponsors have begun offering prizes for fast performance, threatening the redundancy that keeps testimony reliable.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Garden Record Burnings
entries.body:
Soldiers burned channel rolls while calling them rebel lists. Some officers preserved copies to assess taxes afterward. Those administrative duplicates now undermine the official claim that destroyed gardens had been abandoned, revealing continuity through records never intended as memorials.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Rootstock Plaque
entries.body:
A burial plaque was carved on the reverse of an irrigation marker. Its older face names gardeners excluded from the monument’s history. Removing it would destabilize a stair, so conservators propose a supported opening that permits inspection without sacrificing the present structure.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Supported Finish
entries.body:
A runner may finish leaning upon another without disqualification. The custom honors a relay in which a leading competitor turned back for his exhausted sister. Elite households celebrate brotherly loyalty while objecting when unrelated laborers claim the same allowance.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Songs of Turned Stone
entries.body:
These verses pair missing household names with visible stone reuse. Performers revise a line when evidence contradicts it, preserving corrections in spoken prefaces. Authorities demand a fixed authorized text, overlooking that revision is the repertoire’s safeguard against confident falsehood.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Terrace Honey Moth
entries.body:
Small moths pollinate night-blooming terrace herbs and breed in dry retaining joints. Restoration plaster can destroy their refuges. Gardeners negotiate staggered repairs, while ceremonial patrons seek immaculate walls whose appearance would damage the gardens sustaining the custodians.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Breath Ladder Route
entries.body:
A zigzag path breaks the necropolis climb into intervals matched to sung measures. Injured runners use it more than ceremonial stairs. Officials charge pilgrim tolls here too, prompting a petition distinguishing practical access from participation in a sponsored observance.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Testimony in Measure Rule
entries.body:
A sung account may establish a question requiring investigation, though it cannot alone transfer land. Families value recognition of their repertoire; patrons portray the rule as proof the songs are unreliable. Readers answer that written accusations face the same evidentiary limit.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Winter of Unmarked Burials
entries.body:
Frozen garden soil forced survivors to share improvised graves outside the formal terraces. Later officials counted the lack of monuments as absence of inhabitants. Household fuel records document mourners cooking beside the graves and supply a different population history.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Relay Water Flask
entries.body:
Its narrow mouth limits rapid drinking and preserves water for a partner. A celebrated flask is claimed by three runner families. An old repair places it in a communal workshop, suggesting its significance arose through shared use rather than exclusive ownership.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Name Before the Prize
entries.body:
Presenters recite the carried names before announcing relay winners. Sponsors try to shorten the recital for distant guests. Organizers offer printed summaries only as aids, insisting that the people whose absence justifies the gathering cannot become optional introductory material.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Gardeners’ Countercalendar
entries.body:
The calendar dates the campaign by graft failures and harvest interruptions rather than rulers’ reigns. Scholars use it to reconcile inconsistent official dates. Gardeners object when their observations are credited to a prestigious reader without naming the households that kept them.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Returning Refrain
entries.body:
Wind moving through an opened stair produces the rhythm of a famous refrain. Musicians disagree about the similarity. Masons reproduce it with measured airflow, showing that a natural mechanism can sustain meaningful remembrance without proving the missing singers are speaking.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Terrace Wall Grafting
entries.body:
Gardeners plant selected roots through wall beds to bind soil, requiring careful pruning so roots do not split masonry. Courts classify this skilled work as ceremonial service. Practitioners seek payment schedules and authority over repairs rather than praise for inherited devotion.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Monuments’ Maintenance Claim
entries.body:
Royal custodians ask displaced descendants to keep repairing walls above their former gardens. Descendants offer finite paid work while demanding accurate inscriptions. The disagreement turns on whether necessary maintenance can be separated from recognition of the structures’ contested origins.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
